title: Meta-iLaD: Identifiable Latent Dynamics via Meta-Learning
one_liner: A model learns hidden states of a time series and can adapt to new situations on the fly by learning how to read clues from a few examples.
lead: When you watch a video of a moving object, your brain tracks invisible things: its speed, direction, and the forces acting on it. Machine learning models face the same challenge—they must learn hidden states that explain what they see in a sequence of data. The problem: if the world's rules change (a ball moves in water instead of air), a model trained on one environment usually fails on the new one. Meta-iLaD solves this by adding a meta-learner that quickly reads the new world's rules from just a handful of examples, so the model works in unfamiliar places.

problem.h2: The gap between learning and adapting
paras: A model watching a time series must guess invisible states that matter: a ball's true position, a stock's true trend, a person's health state. But the model can only see the surface—the measurements the world gives it—and must reverse-engineer the hidden ones. The catch: the world's rules change. A ball's physics differ in air versus water; a stock's behavior differs in normal times versus a crisis. A model trained on one environment learns rules that break when the environment shifts.

A naive approach: label the situation in advance ("this is water motion" or "this is a crisis") and train separate models. This works if you know all situations ahead of time. But it fails when the new situation is one you never prepared for. You are stuck.

callout.html: The paper adds a meta-learner that reads the new world's rules from a few examples, so the model's hidden states stay valid even when the world changes, because the hidden states are tuned to the correct rule-set instead of a stale one.

panels.title: 1. The hidden world
panels.caption: A sequence hides invisible states (position, velocity, force). Model sees only measurements.

panels.title: 2. One environment, one set of rules
panels.caption: Model learns weights (darker bars mean stronger connections) to uncover states when rules are known.

panels.title: 4. Meta-learner reads the few examples
panels.caption: A second learner glances at a handful of data from the new world and figures out what changed.

panels.title: 5. Hidden states stay true
panels.caption: Model uses the new knowledge and keeps tracking the hidden states correctly in the new place.

steps.b: Model sees a time series and guesses hidden states
steps.text: At each moment, the model uses the previous hidden state plus the current measurement to guess the new hidden state.

steps.b: But hidden states can depend on invisible rules
steps.text: Different rules change how states evolve—a ball in air decays speed slowly, in water it decays fast because water is denser. If the model thinks it is in air when it is really in water, it will guess the wrong new state and then all future forecasts are wrong.

steps.b: The meta-learner reads the new world from examples
steps.text: Given a small batch of data from the new world, a separate neural network learns what the new world's rule-set looks like.

steps.b: The model adapts its hidden-state math
steps.text: The meta-learner's reading tells the main model how to adjust so the hidden states match the new world's behavior.

steps.b: Forecasts now work in the new world
steps.text: The model can predict future measurements accurately, even though it has never trained on this world before.

paras: The paper replaces a fixed rule-reader with a learned meta-learner. Instead of requiring you to label each world in advance, the meta-learner glances at a few examples and figures out the rule-set on the spot. This one change lets the model adapt without retraining.

hidden.h2: The hidden rule-set: what makes each world different
hidden.name: the world rule-set (environment variable)
paras: Consider a pendulum swinging. In air, air resistance slowly damps the swing. In water, resistance is much stronger, because water is denser and exerts more drag on the moving object. The difference is invisible but real—it changes how the pendulum's state evolves. The paper calls this invisible difference an 'environment variable' (the actual rule-set that governs the world). It is not a label you hand in; it is a hidden thing the model must discover.

The model measures this hidden rule-set by looking at a few examples of the new world and asking: 'What pattern explains these measurements?' The meta-learner is a small neural network trained to answer that question quickly, from just 3–10 examples. Once it answers, the main model knows how to adjust its hidden-state math.

heat.caption: Darker means more critical to fitting the new world. Highlighted cells drive the meta-learning.

reads.html: The model must read what-kind-of-world-is-this from its immediate surroundings.
The paper estimates the environment variable c by having a meta-learner network rapidly extract it from a small batch (support set) of examples from the new world.

mechanism.h2: Why the meta-learner works: a chain of two models
paras: The trick is a two-step process. The main model (Model A) is built to learn hidden states when you tell it the world's rule-set. The meta-learner (Model B) is built to guess the rule-set when you show it examples. This combination—pairing a state-learner with a rule-set reader—is what this paper contributes.

Here is the chain: You have a new world you have never seen. You give Model B a small batch of data (3–10 frames). Model B answers the question: 'Given this pattern, what rule-set would make this?' Model B outputs its guess (a vector encoding the rule-set). Model A takes that guess and uses it to recompute hidden states, so that those states match the new world's behavior. The forecasts now work because the hidden states are tuned to the real rule-set, not some old guess.

Why does this work? Because the meta-learner is trained across many worlds, it learns to recognize patterns in how different worlds behave. It does not memorize one world; it learns to read ANY world from a few examples. This is 'meta-learning'—learning how to adapt quickly.

stages.s: Main model adjusts its hidden-state math
Hidden states now match the new world

math.h2: The equation: updating hidden states with the learned rule-set
math.words: new hidden state equals the dynamics function applied to the old hidden state and current measurement, using the world rule-set the meta-learner found. The loss penalizes forecasts that are far from the actual next measurement.
math.equation: z_{t+1} = F(z_t, x_t, c) ; loss = sum_t (x_t - x_predicted_t)^2
symbols: the hidden state at time t (what the model thinks is really happening)
the measurement at time t (what we actually observe)
the world rule-set, found by the meta-learner
the dynamics function (a neural network that updates states)
the model's forecast of the next measurement
how wrong the forecast is (squared difference from truth)

worked.title: A tiny worked example with a pendulum in two worlds
lines: World 1 (air): hidden state is [position=0.5, velocity=0.3], c=air. F predicts next state [0.4, 0.25] (damped by air).
World 2 (water): same measurement x, but c=water. F with c=water predicts [0.3, 0.15] (much stronger damping).
The meta-learner glances at 5 frames of pendulum data in water and outputs c=water. Model A uses c=water.
Now forecasts match reality. Without the meta-learner guessing c, forecasts would be wrong by ~50%.

math.note: The meta-learner finds c from examples; F uses c to update the hidden state correctly for that new world.

bars.h2: Forecast accuracy before and after adapting

charts.title: Old approach (fixed rule-set)
charts.note: Without knowing the new world's rules, even guesses based on pre-labels fail badly.

charts.title: Meta-iLaD (meta-learner adapts)
charts.note: The meta-learner reads the new rules from just a handful of examples; forecasts stay accurate.

items.b: Not enough examples to read the new world.
items.html: If the batch is too small (1–2 frames), the meta-learner may misguess the rule-set. The paper shows accuracy drops if you use fewer than 3–5 examples.

items.b: The new world is too different from training worlds.
items.html: If the new world's rule-set is unlike anything the meta-learner trained on, it may not recognize it. The meta-learner cannot guess rule-sets it has never encountered.

items.b: The rule-set is not fully determined by early examples.
items.html: If the new world's behavior only becomes clear after many time steps, the meta-learner will guess wrong from just a few frames. Some worlds are slow to reveal themselves.

items.b: Done right: the meta-learner trains on a diverse set of worlds.
items.html: If training includes worlds with many different rule-sets, the meta-learner learns to recognize a wide range. Forecasts then stay accurate on truly new worlds.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic dataset with two worlds: a pendulum in air (light damping) and a pendulum in water (heavy damping). Train the model on a mix of both. Then, hide one world's data at test time. Given just 5 frames from the hidden world, run the meta-learner to read its rule-set, then forecast the next 20 frames. Measure forecast error.
demo.metric_eq: forecast error = mean squared distance between predicted and true future frames ; adaptation speed = how many examples needed to drop error from 80% (baseline) to 20% (final)
demo.closing: The demo must show that after seeing just 5 examples, the forecast error drops from 80% (when using the wrong rule-set) to under 20% (when the meta-learner has read the true rule-set).
